vignette: Anh, a 26-year-old male of South Eastern Asian descent, works as a bank teller in the heart of the city. His life took an unexpected turn on that fateful morning when a terrorist attack occurred at his workplace, leaving a lasting impact on his mental health and day-to-day functioning. Anh recounts those few harrowing moments with vivid clarity. He was just starting his shift, sorting through stacks of bills and receipts, when the sound of shattering glass and commotion erupted from outside. Moments later, masked individuals stormed into the bank, shouting commands in a language Anh barely understood. Fear gripped him as he tried to stay calm and composed, but the sight of weapons and the panicked faces of his colleagues shattered any semblance of normalcy. The terrorists took several hostages, including Anh, who found himself trembling with fear while trying to remain inconspicuous. The days that followed were a blur of police interrogations, medical check-ups, and constant anxiety about what might happen next. He felt like he was living in a nightmare from which he couldn’t wake up. Anh’s divorce was still relatively recent when the attack occurred, leaving him emotionally vulnerable and isolated. His ex-wife had been supportive at first but eventually grew frustrated with his reluctance to talk about the incident or seek help. Anh found solace in his solitude, but it also contributed to his growing sense of isolation. At work, he struggles with concentration and often feels overwhelmed by the simplest tasks. The bank is a busy place, and the constant noise and movement trigger flashbacks that leave him feeling disoriented and anxious. He avoids looking out of the windows or hearing sirens in the distance, as they remind him of the chaos during the attack. Anh’s sleep has been profoundly affected. Nightmares are frequent, often replaying the events of that day in disturbing detail. He wakes up drenched in sweat, his heart racing from sheer panic. Even when he manages to fall asleep without nightmares, he frequently wakes up feeling unrefreshed and emotionally drained. His eating habits have also changed. Previously a regular eater with balanced meals, Anh now finds himself skipping meals or consuming small portions due to the nausea that accompanies his anxiety. Sometimes, the thought of food turns his stomach as it reminds him of the fear and panic he experienced during those hours in captivity. Anh’s social life has dwindled significantly since the attack. He avoids going out alone and rarely attends gatherings or meets with friends. The prospect of being in crowded places fills him with dread, leading to intense episodes of anxiety that are difficult to manage on his own. Despite his struggles, Anh tries to maintain a sense of normalcy at work. His colleagues have been supportive, but he feels guilty about burdening them with his fears and anxieties. He often finds himself double-checking the security measures in place at the bank, feeling a compulsive need to ensure that such an event never happens again. Anh’s life has become a series of small battles against his own mind. Each day is a struggle to navigate through the triggers that remind him of the traumatic experience. Yet, he still hopes for a future where the fear and anxiety will lessen, allowing him to regain control over his life and find peace in his daily routine. Through it all, Anh remains resilient, holding onto hope that one day the relentless grip of PTSD might loosen its hold on him.
